tagline: A ranch brand links Diamond’s community and its volcanic craters.
intro: The Diamond Loop winds through high-desert habitats, with mountains and sage-covered hills in view. Oregon’s transportation department presents it as the Diamond Loop Tour Route, highlighting wildlife, historic ranches, the Round Barn and volcanic formations. The department gives a distance of 69 miles and a minimum travel time of three to five hours.

The Diamond name began with rancher Mace McCoy’s cattle brand. Settled in 1874–75, the community became a supply center for ranchers, sheepherders and travelers. The ranch’s name spread to the post office and the nearby craters. Peter French built his round barn in the late 1870s or early 1880s for training horses through the winter. A later dispute concerned the volcanic landscape itself: in the 1970s, stonecutters illegally removed lava slabs for building veneer. Diamond Craters received additional protection as an Outstanding Natural Area in 1982.

Begin eastbound on South Diamond Lane through the southern part of Malheur National Wildlife Refuge, a stopping point on the Pacific Flyway. Diamond lies along Swamp Creek at the head of Diamond Valley, northwest of Steens Mountain. Continue north to the Round Barn, then west on Lava Beds Road to Diamond Craters Outstanding Natural Area. There, a self-guided tour highlights Lava Pit Crater and Graben Dome.

moments.title: Diamond
moments.text: Diamond’s name comes from the diamond-shaped branding iron used on a local cattle ranch. Rancher Mace McCoy established the Diamond Ranch, and its name passed to the community, post office and craters. The settlement served ranchers, sheepherders and travelers as a supply center. A post office followed in 1887. The community lies along Swamp Creek, which flows down the valley into Diamond Swamp, part of Malheur National Wildlife Refuge. Diamond Lane links the community with Oregon Route 205, between Frenchglen to the south and Burns to the north. Steens Mountain lies southeast of the community.

moments.title: Pete French Round Barn
moments.text: A covered circular track surrounds the Round Barn’s stone-walled stable, giving horses a place to exercise during winter. Peter French had the barn built in the late 1870s or early 1880s. It is the only surviving round barn of the group once in the vicinity. The barn measures 100 feet across; the stone corral at its center is 60 feet in diameter. Local rock and mud form the circular wall, while lumber came from 60 miles to the north. Juniper posts support the interior. The Jenkins family donated the site to Oregon in 1969.
moments.notice: Juniper posts support the barn around its circular stone-walled stable.

moments.title: Diamond Craters
moments.text: Diamond Craters began with molten basalt spreading in a thin layer across a dry lake bed. Before that layer cooled completely, more magma pushed underneath and raised six domes. In the 1970s, commercial stonecutters illegally removed lava slabs to sell as veneer for fireplaces, houses and chimneys. Geologists objected that slab harvesting and heavy equipment threatened the volcanic field’s research value. Outstanding Natural Area designation added protection in 1982. The volcanic field also contains basaltic lava flows and cinder cones. A self-guided tour highlights Lava Pit Crater, Graben Dome and other features of the volcanic landscape.
